stories.title: SVN Chicago Commercial Facilitates Sale of Property in Chicago’s Noble Square Neighborhood
stories.excerpt: SVN | Chicago Commercial facilitated the $1.56 million sale of a six-unit Greystone and coach house property at 950–952 N. Noble Street in Chicago’s Noble Square neighborhood. Wayne Caplan, Senior Vice President with SVN | Chicago Commercial, represented the seller. The value-add property drew immediate buyer interest, before ultimately selling above asking price. The building’s Noble Square location and potential for further enhancement contributed to the highly competitive process.“Five showings and five offers in a single day speak to the demand for well-located multifamily opportunities in Chicago,” said Caplan. “When quality assets come to market in established neighborhoods like Noble Square, buyers are prepared to move quickly.” Join the industry’s top multifamily decision-makers at Connect Apartments on September 22 in LA. Hear from the investors, developers, lenders, owners, and advisors shaping today’s apartment market through candid conversations, networking, and market insights. Register today at www.connectapts2026.com. The post SVN Chicago Commercial Facilitates Sale of Property in Chicago’s Noble Square Neighborhood appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: SVN Chicago sold six-unit Noble Square property at $1.56M above asking price.
Five offers received in single day signals strong demand for well-located multifamily.
Value-add potential and neighborhood location drove competitive bidding in Chicago market.
stories.summary: SVN Chicago Commercial facilitated the $1.56 million sale of a six-unit Greystone and coach house at 950–952 N. Noble Street in Chicago's Noble Square neighborhood, with the property selling above asking price after receiving five offers in a single day. The competitive process reflects strong investor appetite for value-add multifamily opportunities in well-positioned Chicago submarkets. The deal signals sustained demand for small-to-mid-sized rental properties with enhancement potential in urban neighborhoods.
stories.impact: Noble Square's rapid absorption of this small multifamily asset—and the above-ask pricing—indicates tightening inventory of development-ready land and value-add stock in Chicago's prime urban cores. Developers should accelerate acquisition pipelines in similar transit-adjacent, gentrifying neighborhoods before competition and land costs rise further.

stories.title: CBRE Arranges $11M Refinancing for Minnesota Office Property
stories.excerpt: CBRE has arranged $11 million in refinancing for Grandview Square, a 98,561-square-foot office property in Edina, Minnesota. Billy Mork, Joel Torborg and Mike Vannelli of CBRE Capital Markets’ Debt and Structured Finance team in Minneapolis secured a five-year, fixed-rate, full-term interest-only loan at 5.89% on behalf of Capital Partners, a Minnesota-based commercial real estate investment and management firm. “Grandview Square drew competitive interest because it has the fundamentals lenders are looking for right now, which includes full occupancy, a diverse tenant roster and an owner that has consistently reinvested in the asset,” said Mork. Grandview Square is located at 5201 Eden Ave. in Edina’s Grandview district. The property provides convenient access to downtown Minneapolis, Minneapolis-Saint Paul International Airport and the 50th & France retail corridor. Built in 2001 and renovated in 2025, the property offers a variety of amenities, and the three-story building is 100 percent leased to 16 tenants. The post CBRE Arranges $11M Refinancing for Minnesota Office Property appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: CBRE refinanced $11M office property at 5.89% fixed rate in Edina, Minnesota.
Grandview Square 100% leased to 16 tenants; lender prioritized full occupancy and diversification.
Five-year interest-only loan reflects capital availability for stabilized office despite sector headwinds.
stories.summary: CBRE Capital Markets secured $11 million in five-year, fixed-rate refinancing for Grandview Square, a 98,561-square-foot office property in Edina at a 5.89% rate on behalf of Capital Partners. The property is 100 percent leased with 16 diverse tenants and was recently renovated in 2025. The deal underscores lender confidence in asset quality, full occupancy, and tenant diversification as conditions for capital deployment in the office sector.
stories.impact: This refinance confirms that stabilized, fully-leased office assets with diverse tenant rosters continue to access capital in the Minneapolis market, but at rates reflecting risk premium. For multifamily developers, this signals lingering capital competition from office refinancing; focus acquisition and development capital on markets with stronger multifamily fundamentals and rent growth than office.

stories.title: Vivmark Merger Triggers $742M in Bay Area Apartment Acquisitions
stories.excerpt: The mega-merger of AvalonBay Communities and Equity Residential triggered the purchases of at least seven apartment complexes in the South Bay and East Bay, the Mercury News reported. Affiliates of Vivmark Residential have acquired properties with a combined 1,843 units in Mountain View, Fremont, Campbell, Union City and Dublin for a total of $741.8 million. The largest of the properties by unit count and price was Avalon Campbell at 508 Railway Ave. in Campbell, totaling 348 units and acquired for $147.3 million. Other properties included the following:  Avalon Towers on the Peninsula at 2400 West El Camino Real in Mountain View, 238 units; $140.4-million sale price including an adjacent office building at 2440 El Camino. Avalon Fremont at 39939 Stevenson Common in Fremont; 308 units; $124.3 million. Eaves Creekside at 151 Calderon Ave. in Mountain View; 300 units; $117.3 million. Eaves Fremont at 231 Woodcreek Common in Fremont; 237 units; $88.9 million. Eaves Dublin at 7904 Fall Creek Rd. in Dublin; 204 units; $64.6 million. Eaves Union City at 2175 Decoto Rd.; 208 units; $59.1 million. The post Vivmark Merger Triggers $742M in Bay Area Apartment Acquisitions appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Vivmark affiliates acquired 1,843 units across Bay Area for $741.8M post AvalonBay-Equity Residential merger.
Largest asset: 348-unit Avalon Campbell for $147.3M; portfolio spans Mountain View, Fremont, Union City.
Divestiture activity signals merger compliance and reshaping of ownership in high-cost California markets.
stories.summary: Affiliates of Vivmark Residential acquired at least seven apartment complexes totaling 1,843 units across the South Bay and East Bay for $741.8 million in response to the AvalonBay Communities and Equity Residential merger. The largest purchase was Avalon Campbell, a 348-unit property in Campbell for $147.3 million. The purchases reflect required or strategic divestitures to satisfy merger conditions and represent a significant reshuffling of multifamily ownership in the Bay Area.
stories.impact: AvalonBay-EQR merger-driven divestitures are flooding Bay Area markets with institutional-quality multifamily assets at scales attractive to large operators and funds. Smaller developers should monitor whether any single-site or secondary-market properties surface; consolidation may also constrain future acquisition opportunities as large operators snap up portfolios. Bay Area rents remain strong enough to support these valuations despite broader California multifamily headwinds.

stories.title: KPC Group’s Oceanwide Plaza Bet Started With a Supertall Dream for Manhattan
stories.excerpt: John Petty, senior partner for KPC Group, had just returned from a site visit at Downtown Los Angeles’ infamous “Graffiti Towers,” the beleaguered mega-development that his firm recently began working to resurrect after it stalled about seven years ago. Like so much of the mixed-use project thus far, cleanup was proving to be tougher than expected. The graffiti-covered Oceanwide Plaza development in Downtown Los Angeles. photo: Myung J. Chun / Los Angeles Times The Chinese-funded project became internationally famous for its tagged exterior. On the 250 balconies of the hollow condo-hotel-retail complex, where graffiti artists focused their work during a tagging spree in 2024, cleanup crews found that they took their time. Much of the colorful artwork had a primer coat put down before the spray paint, and, on some of the murals, clear sealant was applied atop the finished work. Each balcony took between 45 minutes and three hours to clean, with some having a few layers of work to scrub. But, during a call with Commercial Observer, Petty said the work is progressing, and expected to finish in time to meet KPC’s agreement to complete cleanup within three months. It’ll eventually result in some new merch KPC hopes to sell in the development’s hotel lobby when and if they finish: Photos taken during cleaning will be turned into a coffee table book featuring imagery of the infamous graffiti. When KPC, helmed by entrepreneur and orthopedic surgeon Dr. Kali Chaudhuri, emerged as a bidder in the auction for what was originally known as Oceanwide Plaza, the paucity of other players chasing the opportunity underscored the challenges of renovation. This was a project many felt was extremely difficult to finance and finesse. But, on July 21, during a bankruptcy hearing in federal court, KPC’s bid was cleared by a judge, giving the firm the opportunity to pay $517 million in cash and credit to acquire the unfinished project. bullets: KPC Group reviving Oceanwide Plaza, Downtown Los Angeles' stalled $1B+ mixed-use 'Graffiti Towers' project.
Graffiti-removal proving complex; each of 250 balconies requiring 45 minutes to 3 hours cleanup labor.
Long-dormant megaproject repositioning signals investor confidence in DTLA market recovery and mixed-use demand.
stories.summary: KPC Group has begun remediation and stabilization efforts on Oceanwide Plaza, the internationally notorious 'Graffiti Towers' in Downtown Los Angeles that stalled approximately seven years ago. The mixed-use condo-hotel-retail complex requires intensive cleanup, with graffiti removal on 250 balconies taking 45 minutes to three hours each due to primer coats and sealant layers. The project represents a major bet on DTLA's long-term viability and mixed-use demand.
stories.impact: Oceanwide Plaza's resurrection, though resource-intensive, signals that even severely distressed megaprojects can attract capital if located in prime urban markets with long-term demand tailwinds. For DTLA-focused multifamily developers, this underscores the competitive pressure from mixed-use and condo-hotel conversions for downtown sites and capital; focus on Class-A rental fundamentals and differentiated positioning to compete with trophy redevelopment plays.

stories.title: Proposed Energy, Digital Infrastructure Project in Pennsylvania Advances
stories.excerpt: Salem 3, a proposed energy and digital infrastructure project in Northeastern Pennsylvania, has continued to advance through the approvals process. The project cleared another hurdle with the Salem Township Planning Commission voting unanimously to recommend an expansion of the township’s existing data center overlay district. For over 200 landowners, the recommendation means they can continue to pursue a potential $1.4 billion land sale involving more than 4,000 acres of working and retired farms, family homesteads and other properties. Approximately 3,000 of the acres involved in the deal will be set aside and remain as natural buffers, green space, and setbacks. Salem 3 would pair existing energy infrastructure with a new generation of data center and related digital infrastructure investment. The project would also require significant privately funded power generation and infrastructure improvements. 4-3 Consulting, a landowner-first development company dedicated to creating strategic assets for the energy and artificial-intelligence industries, is focused on advancing Salem 3 through the required approvals. The post Proposed Energy, Digital Infrastructure Project in Pennsylvania Advances appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Salem 3 data center project in Northeastern Pennsylvania advances toward $1.4B land sale on 4,000 acres.
Salem Township Planning Commission unanimously approved overlay district expansion; ~200 landowners can pursue sales.
Project pairs energy infrastructure with AI-era data center investment; 3,000 acres preserved as green buffer.
stories.summary: Salem 3, a proposed energy and digital infrastructure project in Northeastern Pennsylvania, cleared a major regulatory hurdle when Salem Township Planning Commission unanimously recommended expansion of the data center overlay district. The approval clears the path for approximately 200 landowners to pursue a potential $1.4 billion land sale involving more than 4,000 acres of farmland and residential properties. The project will preserve roughly 3,000 acres as green space while developing new data center and power generation infrastructure.
stories.impact: Large-scale data center and digital infrastructure development in secondary geographies (Northeastern PA) signals emerging competition for regional development sites and labor pools. Multifamily developers should monitor workforce migration and housing demand influx in Northeastern PA and similar emerging AI/energy hubs; early-stage residential development near major infrastructure projects can capture inbound population growth before rents and land costs spike.

stories.title: Advertising Agency Havas Health Expands to 250K-Plus SF in Grand Central District
stories.excerpt: George Comfort & Sons and its partners Loeb Partners Realty and Jamestown have signed Havas Health to a lease expansion that grows its footprint to 254,118 square feet at 200 Madison Ave. The agreement also includes a 15-year extension that will maintain the advertising firm’s presence at the premier Grand Central district office tower through at least 2041. With the 64,657-square-foot expansion, Havas Health’s headquarters will now encompass space across five floors of the 26-story tower.  “Havas Health’s growing long-term commitment to 200 Madison Avenue is a testament to the appeal of the hospitality-focused, amenity-rich environment we are cultivating for our tenants,” said George Comfort & Sons president and CEO Peter S. Duncan. “Havas has been a valued tenant for nearly three decades, and we are proud to support its next chapter of success within the tower.” Duncan and George Comfort & Sons’Alexander Bermingham represented ownership. Havas was represented by Newmark’s David Falk and Jason Greenstein. The post Advertising Agency Havas Health Expands to 250K-Plus SF in Grand Central District appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Havas Health expanded to 254K SF at 200 Madison Ave; signed 15-year extension through 2041.
Major office tenant committed 64,657-SF expansion in Grand Central district; footprint spans five floors.
Long-term lease commitment signals sustained corporate demand for Class-A Manhattan office despite sector volatility.
stories.summary: George Comfort & Sons, Loeb Partners Realty, and Jamestown signed Havas Health to a 64,657-square-foot lease expansion at 200 Madison Avenue in Manhattan's Grand Central district, growing the advertising firm's footprint to 254,118 square feet across five floors. The agreement includes a 15-year extension maintaining Havas's occupancy through at least 2041. The deal reflects sustained commitment from a major tenant to premium Manhattan office space with hospitality-focused amenities.
stories.impact: Havas Health's three-decade presence and aggressive expansion of nearly 25% signals continued tenant stickiness at trophy Manhattan office locations. However, office remains capital-constrained relative to multifamily; developers competing for Central Park South, Grand Central, and similar high-barrier Manhattan submarkets should prioritize residential over office conversions or ground-up projects to capture stronger capital availability and valuations.

stories.title: Aggregate Buys $58M Northern Virginia Portfolio
stories.excerpt: The owner of an 11-building industrial and retail portfolio in Northern Virginia has sold the assets for $58 million. Fairfax-based Aggregate Real Estate Investors acquired the 320,000-square-foot portfolio from Clarke-Hook Corporation. The portfolio includes four business complexes in Fairfax and Loudoun counties that combined were 94 percent leased to more than 90 tenants at the time of the transaction. The tenant mix includes retailers, restaurants, service providers, manufacturers, logistics companies and automotive-related businesses. The largest asset is West Fairfax Commerce Center, a six-building industrial complex totaling about 150,000 square feet at 14506 Lee Road in Fairfax. The deal also includes University Commerce Center in Ashburn, which consists of three buildings totaling approximately 106,000 square feet of retail and commercial office space. Aggregate also acquired the 40,529-square-foot Dulles Trade Center in Sterling, near Washington Dulles International Airport, and the 17,200-square-foot McLean Commerce Center on Chain Bridge Road. Dulles Trade Center is occupied by third-party logistics tenants, while McLean Commerce Center is leased to several local service-oriented businesses. “These properties are substantially leased by stable, creditworthy tenants and provide a strong foundation for long-term ownership where our team can create additional value,” Greg Jacobsen, managing principal at Aggregate, said in a statement. The firm plans aesthetic upgrades and new management initiatives across the portfolio while targeting more value-add deals in the region. Aggregate focuses on open-air retail and industrial assets throughout the Mid-Atlantic. Gregory Cornfield can be reached at gcornfield@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Aggregate Real Estate acquired 11-building portfolio in Northern Virginia for $58M; 320K SF industrial/retail.
Portfolio 94% leased to 90+ tenants across Fairfax and Loudoun counties; mixed retail, manufacturing, logistics.
West Fairfax Commerce Center (150K SF) is largest asset; deal also includes Dulles Trade Center near airport.
stories.summary: Fairfax-based Aggregate Real Estate Investors acquired an 11-building industrial and retail portfolio from Clarke-Hook Corporation for $58 million, comprising 320,000 square feet across Fairfax and Loudoun counties. The portfolio was 94 percent leased to more than 90 tenants including retailers, restaurants, manufacturers, logistics companies, and automotive businesses. The largest asset, West Fairfax Commerce Center, totals 150,000 square feet; the deal also includes University Commerce Center in Ashburn and Dulles Trade Center near Washington Dulles International Airport.
stories.impact: Strong portfolio acquisition by a local operator in Northern Virginia indicates robust industrial and logistics tenant demand, likely driven by proximity to Dulles, defense contractors, and Northern Virginia's data center cluster. Multifamily developers in Fairfax, Loudoun, and Ashburn should note sustained commercial tenant demand and employer stability; these markets offer steady job-growth tailwinds supporting multifamily lease-up and rent growth. Consider industrial-adjacent residential or mixed-use development near logistics hubs.

stories.title: Dwight Supplies $70M Refi on Newark Multifamily Tower
stories.excerpt: New Jersey developer Yisroel Berger has sealed a $70 million loan to refinance a newly redeveloped multifamily tower in Newark, N.J., Commercial Observer has learned. A fund managed by Dwight Investment Management, a registered investment adviser affiliated with Dwight Capital, provided the nonrecourse, interest-only loan for the 216-unit Cosmo 440 project in Newark’s South Ward neighborhood. The development previously received a $60 million loan from BridgeInvest last year for gut renovation of the building, which was constructed in 1969 and has sat empty for a decade, Jersey Digs reported at the time. Dwight’s Alex Izso and David Scheer originated the loan. “Cosmo 440 has revitalized Newark’s Southward, transforming a long-vacant tower into a stabilized, amenity-rich community well positioned near transit and Newark Liberty International Airport.” Izso and Scheer said in a statement. Located at 440 Elizabeth Avenue, the 25-story building consists of 48 one-bedroom apartments, 120 two-bedroom units and 48 three-bedroom floor plans with 26 of the residences set aside as affordable housing. Community amenities include a concierge, coworking lounge, fitness center, playground and parking garage with electric vehicle charging. Drew Capital’s Akiva Drew negotiated the debt for both loans. “We’ve worked with the ownership and the property from the construction phase, through lease-up and now into its next stage of financing,” Drew, founder and principal of Drew Capital, said in a statement. “Executing successfully requires understanding every dimension of the deal.” Berger did not immediately return a request for comment. Andrew Coen can be reached at acoen@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Dwight Investment Management closed $70M refi on 216-unit Cosmo 440 tower in Newark, New Jersey.
Nonrecourse, interest-only loan on South Ward development; prior $60M construction loan from BridgeInvest.
Asset revitalized 1969 building vacant for decade; proximity to transit and Newark Liberty airport.
stories.summary: New Jersey developer Yisroel Berger sealed a $70 million nonrecourse, interest-only loan from a Dwight Investment Management-affiliated fund to refinance the newly redeveloped Cosmo 440, a 216-unit multifamily tower in Newark's South Ward neighborhood. The 25-story building underwent gut renovation and was previously refinanced via a $60 million construction loan from BridgeInvest. The property is strategically located near transit and Newark Liberty International Airport.
stories.impact: Dwight's willingness to deploy $70M on a repositioned Newark multifamily asset signals growing lender confidence in New Jersey urban submarkets and transit-adjacent development. For Northeast multifamily developers, this validates the investment thesis for gut renovations of dormant urban towers in secondary metros with strong transit access; access to capital exists for well-executed deals, though expect stabilization-focused underwriting and possibly higher leverage requirements than boom-cycle terms.

stories.title: Cortland Sells West Palm Rental at Discount for $208M
stories.excerpt: Multifamily development firm Cortland sold a garden-style rental complex in West Palm Beach, Fla., for $208 million, property records show. The transaction ranks among South Florida’s largest multifamily sales this year, although it marked a discount for the Atlanta-based seller. Fairfield Residential bought the 812-unit asset, called Portofino Place Apartments. The property houses 34 three-story buildings across nearly 40 acres at 4400 and 4600 Portofino Way, between North Military Trail and Interstate 95.. The deal equates to about $256,200 per apartment and occurred through two deeds. One, valued at $108 million, covered 416 units built in 2003. The other, valued at $100 million, covered the remaining 396 apartments, which were built in 2006. The buyer nabbed just over $178 million in financing, assuming two loans, with $93.1 million and $85 million respectively in outstanding debt. Both loans, which are backed by Freddie Mac, are scheduled to mature in September 2033. Cortland purchased the complex for a combined $229 million in 2021, during the height of the pandemic when rents skyrocketed. The nearly $20 million loss is likely in part due to rent growth having slowed since then. The recent sale follows another big sale from Cortland. In May, it sold the 456-unit Uptown Boca Villas for $240 million to the real estate investment arm of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. The deal remains South Florida’s largest multifamily sale so far this year. Representatives for Cortland and Fairfield Residential did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Julia Echikson can be reached at jechikson@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Cortland sold 812-unit Portofino Place (West Palm Beach) to Fairfield Residential for $208M; below 2019 basis.
Garden-style asset split into two tranches: 416 units at $108M (2003) and 396 units at $100M (2006).
Sale-leaseback: buyer assumed $178M Freddie Mac debt maturing September 2033; equates to $256K per unit.
stories.summary: Cortland sold Portofino Place Apartments, an 812-unit garden-style complex in West Palm Beach, Florida, to Fairfield Residential for $208 million—a discount relative to Cortland's prior $229 million acquisition price. The property spans 40 acres across 34 three-story buildings and was divided into two purchase tranches (416 units and 396 units) valued at $108 million and $100 million respectively. Fairfield assumed approximately $178 million in existing Freddie Mac debt, with loans maturing in September 2033, translating to approximately $256,200 per unit.
stories.impact: Cortland's below-cost sale of a stabilized, fully-leased South Florida multifamily asset reflects portfolio repositioning and potentially softer investor appetite for garden-style product in high-growth but competitive Florida markets. For developers, this signals market saturation risk in West Palm Beach; acquisition prices for Class-B and Class-C product are compressing amid elevated construction costs and cap-rate volatility. Focus new development on premium locations with defensible unit economics and consider distressed-sale opportunities in secondary Florida markets where pricing dislocation is pronounced.

stories.title: Westbridge Realty Group Files Plans for Three 99-Unit Buildings in the Bronx
stories.excerpt: New York City-based real estate development firm Westbridge Realty Group has filed plans to build three 99-unit residential buildings on a development site in the Bronx’s Soundview neighborhood, the latest example of the trend to cap multifamily projects at 99 units to reap maximum benefit from the city’s 485-x tax incentive. Steven Westreich, president and founder of Westbridge, filed plans this week with the New York City Department of Buildings (DOB) to build a 13-story, 99-unit residential building at 851 Rosedale Avenue; a 13-story, 99-unit building at 831 Rosedale Avenue, also known as 600 Noble Avenue; and a 12-story, 99-unit building at 863 Soundview Avenue, also known as 829 Soundview Avenue. If approved, the projects would produce a total of 297 units in Soundview. The project at 851 Rosedale Avenue would include nine apartments on each of the third through 13th floors, as well as 50,687 square feet of commercial space and rooftop space, according to the DOB filing. The other two buildings would also each feature 50,687 square feet of commercial space, but further amenities were unclear. 851 Rosedale Avenue and 829 Soundview Avenue are adjacent properties, while 831 Rosedale Avenue is a block south. Leandro Nils Dickson is listed as the architect for each building filing. Spokespeople for Westbridge and the architecture firm did not immediately respond to requests for comment. While it’s unclear whether Westbridge plans to build the project using the 485-x tax abatement, signs point to yes due to the 99-unit nature of the filings. Many developers across New York City have capped their projects at 99 units to avoid what they say are expensive construction wage mandates under the 485-x abatement for projects with 100 or more units. There’s plenty of those 99-unit projects in the Bronx alone. bullets: Westbridge Realty filed plans for three 99-unit buildings in Bronx's Soundview neighborhood; total 297 units.
Development strategy exploits NYC 485-x tax incentive cap of 100 units to maximize subsidy value.
Projects include 13-story, 13-story, and 12-story residential buildings with commercial space on Rosedale and Soundview Avenues.
stories.summary: Westbridge Realty Group filed plans with NYC's Department of Buildings to construct three residential buildings in the Bronx's Soundview neighborhood, each capped at 99 units to maximize the city's 485-x tax incentive program. The projects include two 13-story, 99-unit buildings at 851 and 831 Rosedale Avenue and one 12-story, 99-unit building at 863 Soundview Avenue, for a combined 297 units. The Rosedale Avenue project also includes 50,687 square feet of commercial space.
stories.impact: The 99-unit cap strategy reflects widespread developer optimization of NYC 485-x incentive structure, creating a pipeline of smaller-scale multifamily projects across the Bronx and outer boroughs. This modularization of development—three separate 99-unit projects rather than a single 300-unit tower—increases entitlement and financing complexity but unlocks incremental tax benefits. For competing Bronx developers, this signals accelerating deal velocity in Soundview; move aggressively on adjacent sites and be prepared to compete on subsidy optimization and timeline, not just construction quality.
